paragraphs: It has been argued, in different forms, that a Constitution of the kind proposed by the Convention cannot operate without the aid of a military force to carry out its laws. Like most other things alleged on that side, however, this rests on mere general assertion, with no precise or intelligible statement of the reasons behind it. As far as I have been able to guess the hidden meaning of the objectors, it seems to start from an assumption that the people will be unwilling to see federal authority exercised in any matter of an internal nature. Setting aside any objection that might be raised to the inaccuracy and vagueness of the distinction between internal and external, let us ask what ground there is for assuming that unwillingness in the people. Unless we assume at the same time that the powers of the general government will be worse administered than those of the State governments, there seems to be no room for presuming ill will, disaffection, or opposition in the people. I believe it may be laid down as a general rule that their confidence in a government, and their obedience to it, will commonly be proportioned to the goodness or badness of its administration. It must be admitted that there are exceptions to this rule, but they depend so entirely on accidental causes that they cannot be considered to have any bearing on the intrinsic merits or demerits of a constitution. These can be judged only by general principles and maxims.

Various reasons have been suggested in the course of these papers for thinking it probable that the general government will be better administered than the individual State governments. The principal ones are these. Enlarging the spheres of election will give the people a wider range of choice. Through the State legislatures, which are select bodies of men and which are to appoint the members of the national Senate, there is reason to expect that this branch will generally be composed with particular care and judgment. These circumstances promise greater knowledge and more extensive information in the national councils. They also promise that those councils will be less likely to be tainted by the spirit of faction, and more out of reach of those occasional ill humors, or temporary prejudices and inclinations, which in smaller societies often contaminate the public councils, bring about injustice and oppression of one part of the community, and breed schemes that, though they gratify a momentary inclination or desire, end in general distress, dissatisfaction, and disgust. Several additional reasons of considerable force to strengthen that probability will occur when we come to examine more critically the internal structure of the edifice we are invited to erect. It will be enough to remark here that, until satisfactory reasons can be given for thinking that the federal government is likely to be administered in a way that makes it odious or contemptible to the people, there can be no reasonable ground for supposing that the laws of the Union will meet any greater obstruction from them, or will need any other methods of enforcement, than the laws of the individual members.

The hope of impunity is a strong incitement to sedition, and the dread of punishment is a proportionately strong discouragement to it. The government of the Union, if it has a proper degree of power, can call to its aid the collective resources of the whole Confederacy. Will it not be more likely to suppress the FORMER feeling and to inspire the LATTER than the government of a single State, which can command only the resources within itself? A turbulent faction in a State may easily suppose itself able to contend with the friends of the government in that State. But it can hardly be so infatuated as to imagine itself a match for the combined efforts of the Union. If this reflection is sound, there is less danger of resistance to the authority of the Confederacy from irregular combinations of individuals than to the authority of a single member.

I will here venture an observation that will be no less just because to some it may seem new. The more the operations of the national authority are mixed into the ordinary exercise of government; the more the citizens are used to meeting it in the common events of their political life; the more familiar it becomes to their sight and feelings; and the further it reaches into those matters that touch the most sensitive chords and set in motion the most active springs of the human heart: the greater will be the probability that it will win the respect and attachment of the community. Man is very much a creature of habit. A thing that rarely strikes his senses will generally have little influence on his mind. A government that is always at a distance and out of sight can hardly be expected to engage the feelings of the people. The inference is that the authority of the Union, and the affections of the citizens toward it, will be strengthened rather than weakened by its extension to what are called matters of internal concern, and that it will have less occasion to resort to force in proportion to the familiarity and breadth of its activity. The more it circulates through those channels and currents in which the passions of mankind naturally flow, the less it will need the violent and dangerous expedients of compulsion.

One thing, at all events, must be plain: a government like the one proposed would stand a much better chance of avoiding the necessity of using force than that kind of league which most of its opponents argue for, whose authority would operate only on the States in their political or collective capacities. It has been shown that in such a Confederacy there can be no sanction for the laws but force; that frequent failures of duty by the members are the natural offspring of the very frame of the government; and that whenever these happen, they can be remedied, if at all, only by war and violence.

The plan reported by the Convention extends the authority of the federal head to the individual citizens of the individual States. It will thereby enable the government to use the ordinary public officials of each State in carrying out its laws. It is easy to see that this will tend to wipe out, in the common mind, any distinction between the sources from which the laws might come. It will give the federal government the same advantage in securing due obedience to its authority that the government of each State enjoys, in addition to the influence on public opinion that will result from the important fact that it has power to call to its assistance and support the resources of the whole Union. It deserves particular attention here that the laws of the Confederacy, as to the ENUMERATED and LEGITIMATE objects of its jurisdiction, will become the SUPREME LAW of the land, and that all officers, legislative, executive, and judicial, in each State will be bound to observe them by the sanctity of an oath. Thus the legislatures, courts, and public officials of the individual members will be incorporated into the operations of the national government AS FAR AS ITS JUST AND CONSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY EXTENDS, and will be made auxiliary to the enforcement of its laws.(1) Anyone who follows out for himself the consequences of this situation will see good ground to expect a regular and peaceable execution of the laws of the Union, if its powers are administered with a common share of prudence. If we choose arbitrarily to suppose the contrary, we may draw any inferences we please from the supposition. It is certainly possible, by an unwise exercise of the authority of the best government that ever was or ever can be established, to provoke and drive the people into the wildest excesses. But suppose the adversaries of the proposed Constitution presume that the national rulers would be insensible to the motives of public good or to the obligations of duty. I would still ask them how the interests of ambition, or the aims of encroachment, can be advanced by such conduct.
1. The sophistry that has been used to show that this will tend to the destruction of the State governments will be fully exposed in its proper place.
